slides.title: Try, then roll back
slides.subtitle: Kernighan–Lin refinement · pair swaps and the best prefix
slides.transcript: This module covers Kernighan–Lin (KL) refinement: given an initial grouping with fixed side sizes, how to lower the wiring across it by swapping pairs. Three ideas are at its core: why a pair gain subtracts 2w, why negative gains are tried too, and why only the best prefix is kept in the end.

slides.title: The problem
bullets: Input: an undirected weighted graph and an initial bisection with fixed side sizes
Move: swap one pair, a (left) and b (right)
Goal: make the cut (total weight across) smaller
Constraint: the node count per side never changes
Output: the trial sequence, the best prefix, the accepted grouping and the stop reason
slides.note: A fixed head count ≠ area balance: with cells of different areas, swapping two nodes can unbalance the area.
slides.transcript: The input is an undirected weighted graph and an initial bisection. Here the seed puts A and E on the left and B, C, D on the right; the edges across are AB, AC, CE and DE, so the cut is 12. KL only allows one-for-one swaps, so the node count on each side never changes. Note that this balances the count of nodes, not their area.

slides.title: Background and place
lines: Take a decent grouping, then improve it step by step.
KL was proposed by Kernighan and Lin in 1970 (Bell System Technical Journal), a classic heuristic for improving a bisection.
In this course it follows Module 06: spectral bisection gives the initial grouping and KL improves it locally; Module 08’s FM then replaces the pair swap with single moves.
slides.transcript: KL is a heuristic published by Kernighan and Lin in 1970 in the Bell System Technical Journal. Rather than grouping from scratch, it improves an existing bisection. In this course it follows spectral bisection: first an initial grouping, then local improvement. The next module, FM, moves one node at a time instead of one for one.

slides.title: The cut and D values
bullets: D(v) = external weight − internal weight
External: v’s edges to the other side; internal: v’s edges to its own side
D(v) is how much the cut drops if v alone moves across
The larger D, the more v “wants” to cross
slides.transcript: First give every node a number, D. External weight is its edges to the other side; internal weight is its edges to its own side. Both of A’s edges go across, so D(A) is 6 minus 0, which is 6. C has only 2 external and 6 internal, so D(C) is minus 4: it would rather stay.

slides.title: The pair gain
bullets: The gain of swapping a, b: g = D(a) + D(b) − 2w(a,b)
One node from each side: 2 × 3 = 6 pairs
Largest: A↔D, 6 + 3 − 0 = 9
Ties go by the lexicographic order of (−g, a, b)
slides.transcript: The gain of swapping a pair a, b is D(a) plus D(b), minus 2w(a,b). Two nodes on the left and three on the right make six pairs. The largest in the table is A and D: 6 plus 3 minus 0, which is 9.

slides.title: Why subtract 2w
bullets: Both D values count edge DE (weight 5) as “external”
After the swap E and D are still on opposite sides: DE is still cut
The extra must come back off: 2 × 5 = 10
slides.transcript: Why subtract 2w? Look at E and D. D(E) plus D(D) is 9, but both D values count edge DE as external, once each. After the swap, E is on the right and D on the left: still on opposite sides, so DE is still cut. The edge’s contribution must come off twice, so g is 9 minus 10, which is minus 1.

slides.title: Step one: a trial swap, then lock
bullets: Pick the largest-gain pair: A↔D, g = +9
After the swap, cut 12 → 3
A and D lock: they don’t move again this pass (dashed rings)

bullets.text: This is still a “trial”, not yet accepted

slides.transcript: Step one picks A and D, the largest gain; after the swap the cut drops from 12 to 3. The two swapped nodes lock and don’t move again this pass. Note that this step is only a trial for now; it has not been accepted.

slides.title: Step two: take the negative gain too
bullets: Recompute D: the candidates left are E↔C −8, E↔B −13
KL does not stop at the first negative gain
It still takes the largest, E↔C: the cut rises to 11 for now
No unlocked node is left on the left: the pass’s trials end
slides.note: Why take a negative gain? On a bigger graph, a step that first makes things worse can be followed by a larger positive gain; only a finished pass shows it.
slides.transcript: After recomputing D, both remaining candidates have negative gains. KL does not stop here; it takes the largest anyway, E and C, gain minus 8, and the cut rises to 11 for now. With no unlocked node left on the left, the pass’s trials end.

slides.title: The best prefix and roll-back
bullets: Cumulative gains: k=0 → 0, k=1 → +9, k=2 → +1
Take the largest, consecutive prefix only: k* = 1
From the pass start, apply only the first step

bullets.text: Accept ABC | DE, cut = 3; step 2 is undone

slides.transcript: At the end of the pass, look back at the cumulative gains: doing nothing is 0, the first step is plus 9, both steps are plus 1. The largest is the first step alone, so from the pass start only the A–D swap is applied, and the accepted grouping is ABC versus DE, cut 3. Step two is undone: it was only there to see whether anything better came after it.

slides.title: Pass two: the empty prefix and the stop
bullets: Start from ABC | DE, everything unlocked
Trials: E↔C −8, D↔B +2
Cumulative −8, −6: neither beats doing nothing

bullets.text: The best prefix is empty (k = 0) → the algorithm stops

slides.transcript: Pass two starts from ABC versus DE with every node unlocked again. The two trial steps gain minus 8 and plus 2, cumulative minus 8 and minus 6, and neither beats doing nothing. The empty prefix wins, the cut stays 3, and the algorithm stops.

slides.title: The pseudocode, line by line
bullets: Lines 1 and 8: pass after pass, until the best prefix is empty
Lines 3–5: take negative gains too; after a swap, lock and update D
Lines 6–7: roll back to the start and apply only the best prefix
Each node swaps at most once per pass
slides.transcript: The outer loop of the pseudocode is one pass after another. Inside, while both sides have unlocked nodes, it picks the largest-gain pair, swaps, locks and updates D, taking negative gains too. At the end of the pass it takes the prefix with the largest cumulative gain and applies only those steps from the pass start. If the best prefix is empty, it stops.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Forgetting −2w: computing g(E,D) as +9 and thinking E↔D pays
Stopping at a negative gain: ending pass 1 after cut 3, without seeing every prefix
Taking “any positive steps” as the prefix: a prefix is consecutive from step 1
Reporting the trial state: cut 11 instead of the rolled-back 3
Thinking count balance is area balance
slides.transcript: There are five common mistakes. First, forgetting to subtract 2w, which makes the E–D swap look like plus 9. Second, stopping at a negative gain, which hides the full set of prefixes. Third, a prefix must be consecutive from the first step; you cannot pick out the positive steps. Fourth, don’t report the trial state as the result. Fifth, count balance is not area balance.

slides.title: Scope and limits
bullets: KL is a heuristic: cut 3 on this graph does not mean it finds the global optimum in general
The result depends on the initial grouping: compare methods from the same seed
Each step scans every cross pair: about O(n²) per step, naively
It keeps only the node count per side; different cell areas need their own constraint
In EDA it is often the local-improvement step of partitioning
slides.transcript: KL is a heuristic. Getting cut 3 on this small graph is a property of this graph, not a promise of the global optimum. It depends on the initial grouping, so different methods should be compared from the same seed. A naive implementation scans every cross pair at each step. It only balances the head count; different cell areas need separate handling.

slides.title: Summary
lines: A trial may make things worse; acceptance looks only at the best prefix.
Pair gain g = D(a) + D(b) − 2w(a,b); lock each pass, roll back, repeat; stop on the empty prefix.
Next module, FM: move one node at a time, with a balance window instead of “one for one”.
slides.transcript: In summary: a trial may make things worse, but acceptance looks only at the best prefix. A pair gain subtracts 2w; each pass locks the swapped nodes and rolls back to the best prefix at the end; if that prefix is empty, stop. The next module’s FM moves one node at a time, with a balance window instead of one for one.
